title: Ninety-nine names
hookLine: the Prophet ﷺ said Allah has ninety-nine names and whoever learns them enters the garden (Bukhari)

cards: A misbaha, a string of Muslim prayer beads, slips through the fingers one bead at a time.
Count them and you may find ninety-nine, sometimes split into three groups of thirty-three by two small markers, or thirty-three, meant to go around three times.

They hang from taxi mirrors in Cairo and from kitchen hooks in Dearborn. That number isn't random. It comes from a single sentence of the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ, recorded by both Bukhari and Muslim, with a promise attached.
And scholars have turned that sentence over, lovingly, ever since: what the number means, and what it means to know the names.

teach.b: Here's the hadith, in paraphrase. Allah has ninety-nine names, one hundred minus one.
Whoever ahsaha them will enter the Garden. And then: He is odd, witr, and He loves what is odd. Everything turns on one verb, ahsaha.
At its simplest it means to count, to number off. But the scholars didn't stop at counting.
Some said it means to memorize them; others, to understand them; others, to live by them, so that knowing the Merciful makes you merciful, and knowing the Patient makes you patient.
Some said a real ahsaha holds all of these. Counting is the door. Living is the house.

teach.h: THE NUMBER, BUT NOT THE LIST.
teach.b: Then a surprise: the hadith gives the number, but not the list.

The list most people learn, sung in schools and printed on posters, comes from a report in Tirmidhi's collection, and hadith scholars such as Ibn Hajar discussed whether a narrator added it rather than the Prophet speaking it.
Other early lists differ by a few names. A du'a recorded by Ahmad even asks Allah by every name He has, including names He has kept hidden in His own knowledge.
So scholars such as an-Nawawi read the hadith this way: not that Allah has only ninety-nine names, but that ninety-nine come with this promise.
Ninety-nine doors, and more behind them.
The path takes a first selection, one at a time.

how: Muslims often learn a recited list of the ninety-nine names as children, sometimes set to a melody, and use prayer beads of ninety-nine or thirty-three to remember Allah by His names after prayer.

o: the names of the prophets in the Qur'an
names of God that come with a promise
the complete list of every name God has

games.q: what's inside the hadith — tap the pairs.
p: odd; He loves what is odd

s: the hadith in Bukhari and Muslim gives the full list of ninety-nine
it gives the number; the popular list comes from a report in Tirmidhi.
the hadith limits Allah to only ninety-nine names
scholars such as an-Nawawi read it as ninety-nine with this promise, and more beyond them.
scholars read ahsaha as more than counting
memorizing, understanding and living by the names.

games.q: the hadith promises the Garden to whoever ahsaha the names. what did scholars say that asks of you?
o: count, understand and live by them
games.why: counting is the door; knowing and living by the names is the house.

practice: Count on your fingers the names you already know, saying each one quietly and folding a finger: ar-Rahman, ar-Rahim, as-Salam, al-Wadud, al-Hayy, al-Qayyum, maybe al-Ghafur, the Forgiving, or al-Karim, the Generous, from a friend's name.
Don't worry about how many. When you run out, rest your hands open and breathe.

wordCard.voice: Ninety-nine names. The number of names the Prophet said come with the promise of the Garden, for whoever counts, knows and lives by them. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: counted them, encompassed them. the verb the whole hadith turns on.

carryVoice: Your line: ninety-nine doors. Each name you counted is one you've already found. Day two hundred thirty-three.

sources.ref: Sahih al-Bukhari 7392; Sahih Muslim 2677 (ninety-nine names; whoever enumerates them enters the Garden; He is witr)
Musnad Ahmad 3712 (the du'a asking by every name, including those kept in the unseen)
